title: Would you talk to an AI chatbot about your mental health? 1 in 5 people in Singapore already do, AsiaOne survey shows
key_facts: AsiaOne ran an audience poll from 15 May to 18 Jun 2026 with 1,007 respondents about mental health in Singapore.
47 per cent said they were struggling with mental health conditions.
Among those who sometimes or often struggled, talking to an AI chatbot was the fourth most chosen option, after close friends (34%), a mental health professional (26%) and a spouse (21%).
20 per cent of respondents who struggle said they would talk to an AI chatbot, against 15 per cent of those who rarely or never struggle.
23 per cent of women and 17 per cent of men said they would talk to a chatbot.
Clinical psychologist Dr Annabelle Chow warns chatbots can give wrong information, validate unhelpful thinking and create emotional dependency; 'AI psychosis' is not a formal diagnosis.
Singapore's government points people to the official platform mindline.sg.
quote_evidence: AsiaOne conducted an audience poll from May 15 to June 18 on their outlook on mental health in Singapore. The poll garnered 1,007 respondents.

20 per cent of respondents who said they struggle with their mental health indicated that they would talk to an AI chatbot about it, compared to 15 per cent among those who do not or rarely have mental health struggles.

While Dr Annabelle feels that AI chatbots can be useful as a starting point for finding general information or organising one's thoughts, she warned that they may provide inaccurate information, misrepresent studies or generate sources that do not exist.
why_it_matters_hint: A self-selected reader poll hints at how many people lean on chatbots for emotional support, with clinicians warning of risks.
event_date: Poll 15 May to 18 Jun 2026; article 10 Oct 2026
notes: The headline says 'already do' but the poll asked who 'would' talk to a chatbot and was an AsiaOne audience poll (self-selected readers), not a representative national survey, so the headline overstates.
